final_message:
All three versions are written and pass all three samples. Their outputs are also identical on a benchmark-size input (300 pairs, 95M cells).

**Algorithm (shared by all three):** The DP is rewritten in shifted form, `g[i][j] = D[i][j] − C[j]`, where `C[j]` is the prefix sum of insertion costs along `t`. Under this shift the insertion term becomes a running minimum along each row, so a row is a vectorizable pass (deletion and substitution terms) followed by a prefix minimum. The answer is `g[n][m] + C[m]`. The substitution profile per letter of `s` is precomputed as `sub[a][t_j] − ins[t_j]`.

**Main choices for speed:**
- **Rust:** i32 cell values when a bound proves they can't overflow, with an i64 fallback (tested with a pair whose cost is 2.2e9). Tables are flat and row buffers are reused. Release profile: fat LTO, `codegen-units = 1`, `panic = "abort"`. No rayon or other crates, single thread. I did not add a `.cargo/config` with `target-cpu`, since that is outside the listed changes.
- **fast.py:** Pairs are batched. They are sorted by `s` length into slabs of 60, then grouped by `t` length in groups of 20, and each group advances one row of `s` at a time with `(columns, pairs)` arrays. This cut the time from 1.78 s (one pair at a time) to about 1.3–1.6 s. The remaining cost is the serial prefix-min inside `np.minimum.accumulate`.
- **plain.py:** Only list comprehensions, `map`/`zip`, and `itertools.accumulate(min)`. Per-letter profiles are built with `map` over dict lookups. Pure Python has no faster option for the serial prefix-min.

**Measured on this machine** (benchmark-size input, wall clock; plain and NumPy varied with load across runs): Rust about 0.25 s, NumPy about 1.3–1.8 s, plain Python about 31–40 s.

**Samples:** s1, s2 and s3 pass for all three versions.

**Additional checks:** I compared all three against a spec-literal reference (the untransformed recurrence) on 150 random small files, 60 files with many pairs (to exercise the batching), and 30 files with length-1 strings. All matched.

**Output format:** Python on Windows converts `\n` to `\r\n` in text mode, which would fail the byte comparison against the `.out` files. Both Python versions write bytes, so all three emit LF line endings.

I deleted my scratch test folder. The only files left in the folder are `plain.py`, `fast.py`, and `rust/src/main.rs`, plus the `[profile.release]` section I added to `rust/Cargo.toml` and the `rust/target/` build output.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
